thread.title: The Hit To Berkshire Hathaway's Book Value And The Implications For Buffett's Buybacks - Berkshire Hathaway A (NYSE:BRK.A)

author: Jim Sloan
title: The Hit To Berkshire Hathaway's Book Value And The Implications For Buffett's Buybacks - Berkshire Hathaway A (NYSE:BRK.A)
text:
It's obvious that the Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A )( BRK.B ) portfolio of publicly traded stocks has taken a hit along with everything else in the recent downturn. Because of the large positions in Apple ( AAPL ) and large banks, the hit taken by Berkshire since the end of the 3d quarter probably exceeds in percentage terms that of the market as a whole. An examination of the unrealized loss in value of several of Berkshire's largest holdings through Friday September 21 suggests the scale of the decline in portfolio value:
Apple ( AAPL ) - roughly $19 billion Bank of America ( BAC ) - roughly $5 billion American Express ( AXP ) - a bit over $2 billion Kraft Heinz ( KHC ) - a bit under $3 billion US Bank ( USB ) - a bit over a half billion Wells Fargo ( WFC )- about $4 billion That's more than $33 billion in a portfolio valued at $177 billion at the end of the third quarter, and doesn't include the rest of the portfolio which is smaller and probably declined at a bit lower rate. More than half the damage came from Apple alone. It's sufficient to use a rough estimate because the quarter has another few days to run and at the current level of volatility the losses could be increased or decreased substantially.
In its Monday December 24 edition, Barron's (p. 8) estimated that Berkshire's portfolio had fallen by $30 billion since September 30, the last day of the 3d Quarter. The Barron's estimate, however, used numbers that were a week out of date, taken from prices last Monday. Because the missing week was quite eventful in the market, my own guesstimate is that had the quarter and year closed on Friday the losses in Berkshire's portfolio might be more like $36-37 billion. Note that the above 6 positions alone exceed the Barron's estimate.
The Barron's piece, by the way, was a good short take on Berkshire's position in the current market environment - relatively low risk and relatively high potential. It cited the possibility that Buffett may finally be able to make a large acquisition, mentioning GE ( GE ) as a candidate, an investment I rather hope he does not make. It also notes the large role in the portfolio decline played by Apple and Bank of America.
In the larger frame of reference the decline is probably not a big factor in Berkshire's present and future value. In the immediate to short term frame of reference, however, the numbers have an implication for what investors will see in the 4th quarter and full-year earnings statements.
When observing the impact of the large decline of the Berkshire portfolio, it's necessary to bear in mind the change brought about by the FASB - Federal Accounting Standards Board - via ASU (Accounting Standards Update) 2016-01. The effect of ASU 2016-01 is pretty simple. Beginning with Q1 2018 corporations were required to report unrealized gains or losses in investment portfolios as part of income on their earnings statements. That's pretty straightforward. (I should mention that SA member economonoc reminded me that it was an FASB action in 2016 and not, as I had written while suffering a brain cramp, part of the changes in the new tax law.) Buffett dislikes the new rule, the effect of which, he has said, is to make the earnings statement "useless" to readers. He has more or less instructed investors to disregard the effect on earnings stemming from portfolio gains and losses. To do this you just adjust the numbers by omitting the effects of portfolio fluctuations, focusing on operating results.
Changes in portfolio value have always been reflected in book value, of course, but have not historically had profound impact. Buffett warned that investors needed to be ready for gains and losses which contributed as much as $10 billion, up or down, to a quarterly earnings report. That warning was borne out by the 3d Quarter earnings report when about 60% of reported earnings were paper gains in the stock portfolio. Stocks go up and stocks go down. We haven't yet seen what can happen to book value when they go down in a big way. That is about to change.
Book Value And Unrealized Portfolio Losses Realized gains and losses have always been part of earnings statements, and Buffett has always suggested that investors disregard them, adding with the new requirements of ASU 2016-01 an admonition to disregard reported paper gains and losses as well. I do not recall his ever taking on the impact of portfolio gains and losses as a contributor to changes in book value. This is likely to be the year he discusses it.
Paper gains and losses (unrealized, to use the formal term) are recognized on the balance sheet automatically by a change in fair value (ie. market value), properly adjusted to reflect the liability for taxes which would have to be paid in the event they are sold. A major contributor to increase in portfolio value for the trailing 12 months is owing to the fact that the marginal corporate tax rate was reduced by the new tax law from 35% to 21%. That amounts to an instant jump in value of embedded capital gains of about 38.5%, which can be very impactful. Two of Berkshire's largest holdings, Coke and American Express, have a cost basis less than 10% of market price and thus over 90% of market price consists of embedded capital gains.
Realized capital gains held inside corporations are taxed at the same rate as operating earnings, previously 35% but now 21%. Dividends received by corporations are taxed far more lightly, by the way, inverting the relative tax rates for individuals, although the corporate cap gains rate under the new tax law now approximates the long term cap gains rate for individuals. I have noted in earlier articles that the relative corporate tax rates on dividends and long term gains account in part for Buffett's willingness to hold legacy positions which no longer grow much but pay good dividends. But it has another important implication.
Berkshire's portfolio holdings have always repriced quarterly, but wholly owned businesses never reprice, being held on the books at their initial cost. As Berkshire has morphed from an insurance company with a stock portfolio into more of an industrial/financial conglomerate, book value has come to greatly understate its true business value. This has been an underlying principle for Buffett's changing the measure for buybacks from 110% of book value to 120%, and recently to an undisclosed and more fluid hurdle. That hurdle has been stated simply as a significant discount to business value agreed to by Buffett in consultation with Charlie Munger.
Does book value continue to have a major place in the Buffett/Munger calculus? We are about to find out.
Book Value, Business Value, And Look Through Earnings The book value of Berkshire B shares at the end of the the 3d Quarter (September 30) have been reported by various sources variously at between 151 and 154. This discrepancy probably has to do with the share count used. Dividing the A share equivalent book by 1500, the ratio of B share to A shares, I get about 152. Let's use that number.
Let's assume (although another potentially eventful three and a half days of trading remain in 2018) that market value of the total Berkshire portfolio will fall by about $37 billion. This and other numbers could change at the margins when we learn about share reduction due to buybacks in Quarter 4 and what additions he made to the Berkshire portfolio and at what prices. Let's then assume a tax rate of 21% Federal and 6% state and reduce that $37 billion by the 27% offset stemming from reduced tax liability. That would drop the portfolio loss reflected on the balance sheet by about $10 billion to a hypothetical $27 billion.
Then let's trim that reduction in book value by the roughly $7 billion in operating earnings that Berkshire had in the previous quarter. Still being very provisional and hypothetical, that would bring Berkshire's book value down by a net $20 billion. That's coincidentally pretty close to its rise in book value of $22.6 billion over the first three quarters, and a couple of bad market days could bring the two numbers even closer. In effect, the portfolio decline of the last three months may have effectively wiped out Berkshire's increase in book value for 2018.
Most sites have been carrying Berkshire's price-to-book ratio at 125% based on September 30 book value and the current price of $192 per B share. The 4th quarter hit to the stock portfolio will take book value back to $141 dollars per B share. That generates a current price-to-book ratio of almost 140%. That has not traditionally been buyback territory when book value has been a major part of the rationale.
What will Buffett make of this? His many past statements encouraging investors to ignore changes in earnings statements based on short term performance of the public stock portfolio may suggest his view. Even more important is the Buffett concept of "look through earnings" for the stocks Berkshire holds.
What "look through earnings" attempt to do is to level the playing field somewhat between wholly owned companies and stocks traded in the market. In the absence of "look through earnings" the only two value measures for publicly traded companies are market price and dividends paid. What Buffett suggests instead is "looking through" to the earnings and cash flow in order to understand one's holding as if it were a share in an operating business.
The use of "look through" earnings is also a way of aligning value in a holding with the reasons Buffett had for buying it. It is also a pretty good approach for individual investors in general, especially in turbulent markets like the present when a look through to the underlying operational performance can reinforce focus on the fundamentals of the businesses instead of the whims of the market.
Conclusion My best estimate of the way Buffett would look at the change in Berkshire's book value is that he has already formed a concept of the approximate business value contained in his portfolio so that a drop in book value caused by a drop in the portfolio's market price is noted with something like casual disregard. He most likely sees it the same way he sees distortions brought about by reporting paper gains or losses as a part of reported earnings. Ajit Jain hinted at the inside Berkshire view last week when he bought $20 million worth of Berkshire A shares after having disposed of a smaller number a few months back near the recent highs. How different can his thinking be from that of Buffett?
What will be interesting to see in the 4th quarter report and in coming quarters is the relative preference Buffett demonstrates for buybacks of Berkshire shares versus his other alternatives, including adds to some of his current portfolio holdings, new stock additions, or the acquisition of a whole company or companies. I'm watching this closely myself. Do I want my first major add in this downturn to be JP Morgan ( JPM ), Bank of America, or Berkshire itself, in which I already push the envelope for single stock risk? Stay tuned.
Disclosure: I am/we are long BRK,B, JPM, BAC, WFC, USB. it (other than from Seeking Alpha).
